extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, peer reviewers, and researchers studying peer review (psychology/behavioral science)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines, empirical findings, and recommended evaluative practices for refereeing journal manuscripts, with emphasis on how confirmatory bias and other factors affect reviewers' ratings and recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Rating of how relevant the manuscript's topic is to the journal and field (Factor 1 in the study).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured in the study on a 4-point rating scale (poor, marginal, adequate, good). The paper expects topic relevance to be a primary consideration; in the experiment, relevance ratings did not differ across outcome-manipulated groups. Reviewers should judge whether the research question is important and timely for the journal's audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology (methodological adequacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of whether the experimental or methodological procedures are adequate and appropriate for addressing the research question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considered a primary empirical component that ideally should outrank the direction of results; in the study identical methodologies were rated differently depending on whether results supported reviewers' perspectives (positive results were rated as methodologically better than negative results). Methodology ratings strongly covaried with overall recommendations (r = .94), suggesting susceptibility to 'halo' bias. Reviewers should evaluate procedural validity and internal/external validity independently of outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality and clarity of tables, figures, and reported results (Factor 3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rated on the same 4-point scale. In the experiment, data sections supportive of behavior modification were rated as significantly better than critical data sections despite identical formats. Ambiguous data were devalued as lacking scientific contribution. Reviewers should judge clarity, completeness, and accuracy of data reporting, while avoiding outcome-driven valuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion / Interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation of the authors' interpretation of results and the discussion section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper argues discussion should not unduly bias editorial recommendations; reviewers may, however, exercise editorial prerogative in urging authors to recognize alternative interpretations. In the experiment the discussion section had little influence on overall recommendations compared to results direction; reviewers should distinguish between interpretive claims and the underlying data quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall scientific contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgment of the manuscript's contribution to knowledge, theory, or practice (Factor labeled 'scientific contribution').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rated on the 4-point scale. Positive-results manuscripts were judged as having higher scientific contribution than negative-results manuscripts; manuscripts with no results were sometimes rated higher than those reporting data. Reviewers should base this on relevance and methodological soundness, not merely on whether results confirm existing theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary recommendation (editorial decision)
rubrics_metrics.description: Final recommendation to the editor (accept, accept with minor revisions, accept with major revisions, reject).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collected on a 4-point summary recommendation scale in the study. This variable was strongly influenced by the direction of reported results: positive manuscripts typically recommended for acceptance with moderate revisions, negative manuscripts tended toward rejection or major revision, and manuscripts with no results were more generous. Reviewers should ensure their recommendation follows from objective assessment of relevance and methodology rather than confirmatory preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rating scale and scoring convention
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a standardized rating instrument: 4-point rating scales for component factors (poor, marginal, adequate, good) and a 4-point recommendation scale; study scoring conventions for analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the study, ratings were scored on a Likert-type metric (described in the paper), and statistical analyses (ANOVA, contrasts) were applied. Use of explicit, standardized scales facilitates quantitative comparison and reliability assessment. Editors should provide clear rating anchors and scoring rules to referees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blind reviewing / anonymity
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice of keeping reviewers unaware of authorship and institutional affiliation; in blind reviewing the manuscript's components (intro, method, results, discussion, abstract, bibliography) become the sole bases of judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blind review can reduce biases related to author prestige or affiliation, but does not eliminate other biases (e.g., confirmatory bias based on results). The study used blinded referees and manipulated only manuscript content to assess biases. Editors should adopt anonymity practices but be aware of remaining cognitive biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis ordering of manuscript components
rubrics_metrics.description: Epistemological recommendation that relevance and methodological adequacy should outrank data outcome and interpretation in evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper suggests that, given a relevant question and adequate methodology, results of any direction should be of interest; negative (contratheoretical) results may yield more information under a falsificational view. Reviewers should prioritize introduction (research question) and methods when recommending decisions, and treat results as evidence rather than verdicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid confirmatory bias (do not penalize disconfirming results)
rubrics_metrics.description: Principle that reviewers should not discount or discredit findings because they contradict their theoretical perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirmatory bias leads reviewers to emphasize confirmatory data and ignore or be defensive about disconfirmatory evidence; the study found reviewers were strongly biased against manuscripts reporting results contrary to their perspective. The paper recommends procedural changes (e.g., reviewing without seeing results) and conceptual attention to falsification logic to mitigate this bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Option: evaluate relevance and methodology without seeing results
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed procedural change: ask referees to assess relevance and methodology before receiving results or interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This might reduce prejudice against negative results, but introduces other problems: reviewers may show very low agreement and may feel handicapped by missing components; training and editorial strategies would be needed to handle incomplete evaluations. Editors should weigh trade-offs before implementing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure and report interreferee reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess and disclose the degree of agreement among reviewers (e.g., intraclass correlation coefficients).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper treats peer review as an evaluative test and argues for reporting reliability evidence (paralleling APA standards for tests). The study found very low interrater agreement on many factors and large discrepancies between reviewers' self-predicted reliability and observed reliability. Editors should monitor and report reliability metrics and consider them when interpreting reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train reviewers with caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide reviewer training to improve consensus while recognizing risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training might produce better consensus, but consensus might reflect shared ideological/methodological bias rather than objectivity. Any training program should address bias awareness and emphasize independent assessment of relevance and methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect methodological contradictions and errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Careful inspection for internal inconsistencies, logical impossibilities, typographical errors, or contradictions in reported methods and data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The experiment revealed that reviewers' detection of a contradiction (impossible sample size statement) varied with outcome direction (more detection when results contradicted reviewers' views). This illustrates that bias can affect error detection. Reviewers should systematically check for consistency irrespective of whether results confirm expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware halo effects among component ratings
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid allowing a positive or negative valence on one component to color ratings on other components (shared 'common valence').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed strong correlations among component ratings (e.g., methodology and summary recommendation r = .94), suggesting a halo effect. Reviewers should rate components independently and editors should design forms and instructions to reduce halo contamination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider timeliness/punctuality effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Awareness that review return timing may be associated with evaluation negativity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the study, punctual reviews were marginally more negative than tardy ones; mixed-results manuscripts were returned earlier than clear-cut ones. Editors should monitor whether deadlines or time pressures systematically influence tone or verdict and account for this in decision processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial prerogative to request recognition of alternate interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and reviewers may request that authors acknowledge or discuss alternative interpretations but should not let the discussion unduly determine publication decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers can use their editorial role to urge authors to publicly recognize alternate data interpretations; however, this should not substitute for objective assessment of data and methods. The paper recommends separating interpretive persuasion from empirical judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide constructive, substantive feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should aim to give constructive comments, bibliographic leads, and suggestions even when recommending rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study observed many reviewers provided extensive, constructive feedback (bibliographies, reprints, even analysis). Constructive comments improve manuscript quality and are a valued function of peer review; editors should encourage detailed, helpful commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a falsificational perspective in evaluating results
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophical guideline: negative (contrary-to-prediction) results have stronger logical implications and should be valued accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing Popper and others, the paper argues that only negative results yield conclusive logical implications. Reviewers and editors should appreciate the epistemic weight of disconfirming evidence and avoid privileging confirmatory outcomes merely because they align with prevailing theory.
